doc.title: Randy Brecker interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 12, 2022

chapter: Blood, Sweat & Tears and Horace Silver
title: Learning from the first Blood, Sweat & Tears record
summary: Why he left BS&T after one record: John Simon's studio techniques, arrangements, and the shock of playing for huge pop crowds.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Quitting the band: why sidemen left

blocks.x: So I was at Fredonia in the late 60s, early 70s and we wore out the Blood, Sweat & Tears records. And I’m curious, was it a hard decision to leave that band after the first record, even though you went with Horace Silver, is that correct?
Can you remember your thinking at the time?

Well my thinking was, and I remember this really clearly, that I needed to play more. And in Blood, Sweat & Tears I also learned a lot from, particularly from doing the first record. “The Child is the Father to the Man” was produced by John Simon who was a very bright young guy who had produced Bob Dylan and had a lot of success in production and really knew how to do those kind of records. Studio technique. Double tracking the horns. If he wanted you to sing in tune, I’d never seen this, he had Steve Katz [performs vocal exercise] somehow just doing it, things like that that really worked. And he double tracked himself singing. In the background he had all these tricks that I didn’t take notes but I was watching him very carefully because in my head, well maybe some day I’ll be doing a record like this. So I learned an amazing amount about how to build a rock record as you have it — from the bottom up and just the techniques. But at the time, and they were great arrangements, Freddy Lipsius’ arrangements, the band was great. I learned so much about the business just by seeing how many thousands and thousands of kids, you know, loved rock & roll music, pop music, you know I lived a little insular life I suppose in jazz in New York where you had to pull people into the club, making five or ten dollars a night sometimes with the Duke Pearson Big Band or Clark Terry’s band. That’s about how much those gigs would pay at the Half Note. And it was a shock to go out to California and next thing I know I’m playing for thousands of young people kind of had my background so to speak. So it was a difficult decision but © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-
